t.5.28.2: Then the monkey, gazing upon that queen who was like a goddess in the Nandana grove, pondered many kinds of thoughts.
t.5.28.1: The valiant Hanumān too heard all of it exactly as it happened: the threatening of Sītā, and the words of Trijaṭā, and the menaces of the rākṣasīs.
t.5.28.3: She whom many thousands and tens of thousands of monkeys are searching for in all directions, she, this very one, has been found by me.
t.5.28.5: The distinctive nature of the Rākṣasas has been observed, and this city too, as well as the might of Rāvaṇa, this lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.5.28.4: But I, acting as a well-appointed spy assessing the enemy's strength and moving about in secret, have so far observed this.
t.5.28.6: It is fitting to console the wife of that immeasurable one, who is compassionate toward all beings, a wife longing to see her husband.
t.5.28.7: I shall console her, whose face is like the full moon, who has never known sorrow before and who indeed finds no end to her sorrow.
t.5.28.8: For if I go away without consoling this queen, whose mind is stricken with grief, my departure would be a fault.
t.5.28.9: For if I go there, this illustrious princess Jānakī, finding no deliverance, may give up her life.
t.5.28.10: And it is fitting that I should console that mighty-armed one, whose face is like the full moon and who longs to see Sītā.
t.5.28.11: To address her in the presence of the night-roaming demonesses is improper; how indeed is this to be done? For I have fallen into a difficult plight.
t.5.28.13: And if Rāma should ask me, "What words did Sītā speak to me?", what could I answer him, without having spoken with this slender-waisted lady?
t.5.28.12: If she is not comforted by me during what remains of this night, she will without doubt give up her life; of that there is no doubt at all.
t.5.28.14: If I were to go hastily from here without a message from Sītā, Kākutstha, enraged, might burn me up with his fierce gaze.
t.5.28.16: But I, staying here and finding an opportunity amid the rākṣasīs, will gently console her who is so full of anguish.
t.5.28.15: If I should engage my master on account of Rāma, then his coming here together with his army will prove to be in vain.
t.5.28.18: If I utter refined speech like a twice-born, Sītā, taking me for Rāvaṇa, will become frightened.
t.5.28.17: For I am exceedingly small, and above all a monkey; and yet here I shall speak the refined speech of humans.
t.5.28.19: Meaningful words in human speech must certainly be spoken by me; otherwise this blameless lady cannot be consoled.
t.5.28.20: This Jānakī, already terrified before by the rākṣasas, will be seized by fear once more on seeing my form and hearing my speech.
t.5.28.22: And if a cry were raised by Sītā, the host of rākṣasīs, terrible, bearing various weapons and like Antaka himself, would suddenly come together.
t.5.28.21: Then the high-minded, large-eyed lady, seized with terror and taking me for Rāvaṇa, who can assume any form at will, would cry out.
t.5.28.23: Then those deformed-faced ones would surround me on every side and, each according to her strength, would strive both to slay me and to seize me.
t.5.28.24: Seeing me running all about over the branches, the smaller boughs and the trunks of these excellent trees, they would become filled with fear and suspicion.
t.5.28.25: And seeing my form as I roam through the great forest, the rākṣasīs with their misshapen faces would become stricken with fear.
t.5.28.26: Then the rākṣasīs might raise a call to the rākṣasas too, those appointed by the lord of the rākṣasas, in the dwelling of the lord of the rākṣasas.
t.5.28.27: Those, bearing spears, arrows, swords and weapons of every kind in their hands, would swoop down swiftly in this tumult, spreading alarm.
t.5.28.28: Enraged by them and blasting apart the army of the rākṣasas all around me, I might yet be unable to reach the farther shore of the great ocean.
t.5.28.30: Those who delight in violence might even kill this daughter of Janaka; then this undertaking of Rāma and Sugrīva would come to ruin.
t.5.28.29: Or many swift-acting ones, leaping upon me, might seize me; then she would remain without grasping my purpose, and my capture would come about.
t.5.28.31: Jānakī dwells in this region, where the paths are lost, which is surrounded by rākṣasas, encircled by the ocean, and closely guarded.
t.5.28.32: If I were slain or captured by the Rākṣasas in battle, I see no other helper for Rāma in accomplishing his task.
t.5.28.33: And even on reflection I see no monkey who, were I to be slain, could leap across the great ocean that stretches a hundred yojanas wide.
t.5.28.34: I am indeed able to slay even thousands of rākṣasas, but I shall not be able to reach the farther shore of the great ocean.
t.5.28.35: Battles are uncertain, and doubt does not please me. What wise man would turn a task that is free of doubt into one fraught with doubt?
t.5.28.36: If I speak to Sītā, this would indeed be a great fault on my part; yet if I do not speak to her, Vaidehī would give up her life.
t.5.28.37: Even aims already within reach come to ruin when they run counter to place and time, once they fall to a flustered messenger, just as darkness perishes at sunrise.
t.5.28.38: In the gap between what serves the purpose and what does not, even a firm resolve does not shine; for envoys who fancy themselves learned ruin the very tasks entrusted to them.
t.5.28.39: How may the task not be ruined? How may no despondency arise? And how indeed may the leaping of the ocean not prove to have been in vain?
t.5.28.40: "How indeed might she listen to my words and not be alarmed?" Thus reflecting, the wise Hanumān made up his mind.
t.5.28.41: By praising Rāma, her own kinsman, whose deeds are untiring, I will not alarm her, whose mind is fixed upon that kinsman.
t.5.28.42: Offering the auspicious words, consistent with dharma, of Rāma, the foremost of the Ikṣvākus, whose self is well known,
t.5.28.43: Speaking in a sweet voice, I will make her hear all things; I have arranged everything in such a way that she will surely believe me.
t.5.28.44: Thus the greatly glorious Hanumān, stationed among the branches of the tree and gazing upon the beloved lady of the lord of the earth, spoke in many ways words that were sweet and true.
